section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Harmonic Oscillator Model
section_1.content: Briefly introduce the atom as a system where electrons are bound to the nucleus by spring-like restoring forces. Define the natural frequency (ω₀) of these electrons. This sets the stage for how light interacts with matter.
section_1.example: Visualize an electron as a tiny ball attached to a spring; when a light wave hits it, the spring begins to oscillate.

section_2.title: The Origin of Refractive Index: Driven Oscillations
section_2.content: Explain that when an electromagnetic wave hits a material, the electric field drives the electrons to oscillate. These oscillating electrons emit their own secondary waves. The interference between the incident wave and these secondary waves slows down the net phase velocity of the light, creating the refractive index (n).
section_2.example: A group of runners (the light wave) encountering a crowd of people (electrons) who nudge them slightly, causing the overall speed of the group to decrease.

section_3.title: Color Dependence: Dispersion
section_3.content: Introduce the relationship between the light's frequency (ω) and the resonance frequency (ω₀). As ω approaches ω₀, the amplitude of electron oscillation increases, causing a sharper phase shift. Since different colors (frequencies) interact differently with these resonances, n becomes a function of frequency: n(ω).
section_3.example: A musical string resonating: just as different pitches cause different vibrations, different light frequencies 'tug' on electrons with varying intensities.

section_4.title: Visualizing Dispersion: The Cauchy Equation Graph
section_4.content: Present the n(λ) curve. Use a graph where the x-axis represents wavelength (λ) and the y-axis represents the refractive index (n). Show that n is higher for shorter wavelengths (blue light) and lower for longer wavelengths (red light).
section_4.example: The classic glass prism animation: white light entering a prism and separating into a rainbow because each color 'feels' a different refractive index, bending at a unique angle.

section_5.title: Real-world Application: Chromatic Aberration in Cameras
section_5.content: Apply the concept to optical devices. Explain why simple lenses cannot focus all colors at the exact same point due to dispersion, leading to color fringing in images. Introduce 'Achromatic Doublets' as the solution.
section_5.example: A nature photographer noticing a purple 'glow' around the edges of a bird's wings in a photo; explaining that the camera lens failed to focus the blue and red wavelengths on the same sensor plane.

        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Visualizing Dispersion: The Cauchy Equation Graph", [
            "Refractive index varies with wavelength.",
            "Shorter wavelengths bend more than longer ones.",
            "Prisms separate colors due to this dispersion."
        ])
